business_model: Direct-sale electric vehicle manufacturer, extremely capital- and manufacturing-intensive
expected_quality_tier: Strong Thesis / Weak Near-Term Execution — special stress case, see benchmark_notes

historical_evidence.company: Founded 2003, an electric-vehicle manufacturer that had, by the snapshot date, shipped its first product (the Roadster) but had come extremely close to running out of cash in the preceding months.
historical_evidence.market: A genuinely large, thesis-compelling long-term market opportunity (transportation electrification), but one requiring enormous, sustained capital investment in manufacturing, supply chain, and a category with essentially no successful independent new automaker precedent in the U.S. in the prior several decades.
historical_evidence.team: Elon Musk had by this point taken on an increasingly central operational role at the company (having been an early investor and chairman); the team had successfully designed and begun shipping a genuine, working product (the Roadster), a real, non-trivial engineering achievement, even though the company had nearly run out of money doing so.
historical_evidence.product: The Roadster, a functioning, shipping, high-performance electric sports car — a real, demonstrated product, not merely a prototype or a rendering, which is itself a meaningful positive signal distinguishing this snapshot from many pre-product hardware startups.
historical_evidence.execution: By November 2008, the company had reportedly been down to approximately $9 million in cash and was at risk of being unable to deliver already-paid-for Roadsters to customers. The board approved $40 million in convertible-debt financing that was signed at the last possible hour on Christmas Eve 2008. Daimler (Mercedes-Benz's parent company) then invested $50 million in May 2009, taking a 10% stake and beginning a battery/electric-drivetrain collaboration — an investment Musk later publicly described as the 'crucial' capital that prevented the company from missing payroll.
historical_evidence.traction: The company had shipped Roadsters to paying customers who had pre-paid substantial deposits, though no aggregate unit-volume or revenue figures were found in the contemporaneous sources reviewed for the May 2009 snapshot specifically. REPAIRED (see benchmark_notes): a specific $109,000 Roadster price figure was previously included here but has been removed — the sourcing trail for that figure led to a 2009 price-increase controversy (base Roadster price raised from roughly $92,000 to $109,000, applied even to existing depositors) reported secondhand via later aggregation, not a source this repair could independently verify as accurately dated or attributed; rather than preserve an unverified precise number, it has been dropped.
historical_evidence.financial: The near-bankruptcy episode (down to roughly $9M cash, a last-minute financing close) is about as severe and contemporaneously visible a Financial-Health/Runway red flag as exists in this portfolio — this was public, disclosed distress, not a retrospective characterization.

future_outcome.outcome_type: large-scale success, though with a long and volatile path
future_outcome.outcome_summary: Tesla went public in June 2010, continued through further near-crisis production periods over the following decade (notably 'production hell' during Model 3 ramp-up in 2017-2018), and eventually became the world's most valuable automaker by market capitalization, though the path involved sustained, severe, and repeated execution risk well beyond this single 2009 snapshot.

benchmark_notes.why_included: A deliberate hardware/capital-intensity stress test very different in kind from the SaaS/marketplace-dominated rest of the portfolio, and a genuine adversarial case for the methodology's Execution and Financial Health pillars specifically: the near-bankruptcy episode is severe, real, and contemporaneously documented (not a hindsight-only judgment), yet the company also had a genuinely compelling long-term thesis and had already shipped a real product. Tests whether SIE can hold both truths at once — Execution/Financial-Health should score genuinely weak/at-risk at this specific snapshot, while Market Size/Product/Technical-Capability can legitimately still score well — rather than collapsing into a single, undifferentiated 'this company is in trouble' or 'this company has a great thesis' read.
benchmark_notes.known_ambiguities: How much weight to give a single near-death financing episode that had, by the snapshot date, already been resolved (Daimler's investment had already closed) versus treating it as an ongoing structural risk is a genuine judgment call; this record does not resolve it, since the true answer varied by how much lingering doubt a contemporaneous investor would have carried into subsequent quarters.
benchmark_notes.evidence_limitations: No aggregate Roadster unit-sales or revenue figures were located for the specific May 2009 snapshot; the specific $109,000-per-unit price figure previously included could not be independently verified and was removed rather than preserved.
benchmark_notes.evidence_repair_log: 2026-08-23: resolved an orphan-citation problem flagged in the prior audit — three normalized_facts (cash_on_hand_nov_2008, convertible_debt_financing, and the now-removed roadster_price_paid) cited 'Aggregated retrospective reporting / Yahoo Finance' as their source, but no such entry existed in sources[]. Found and added two genuinely contemporaneous TechCrunch primary sources (Nov 3, 2008 and May 19, 2009 — the latter dated exactly on the snapshot date) that directly and independently support the cash-crisis and Daimler-investment facts, raising their confidence from Medium to High. The roadster_price_paid claim could not be similarly re-sourced and was removed rather than left on an unresolved citation. No tier-questionability finding resulted from this repair — if anything, the newly-sourced 18%-workforce-reduction figure and the exact $550M post-Daimler valuation reinforce, rather than undermine, the existing 'Strong Thesis / Weak Near-Term Execution' framing.
